chapter_theme: Wandering through a flowering grove, a garlanded man reaches an asoka and a gem slab, where its keeper explains a priest's foretelling that a prince will come, and the king then sends four women, drawn in their ornaments and killing glances, to attend him.

cast.role: the garlanded man who enters the grove and reaches the slab
the keeper of the asoka and the gem slab
the learned priest whose foretelling the keeper reports
the king who sends the four women
the four goddess-like women sent to attend the guest

431.reading: A catalogue of grove trees in bloom: bakula and mango with honey-drinking bees, naga and punnai dropping flowers on the ground beside them.
431.nuance: The verse is a list in the edition's compressed word division, with its words run together; the trees are named by their usual Tamil names but several identifications are held with doubt.

432.reading: The grove list continues: shady sandal, champak, kurava and asoka, each described by what it spreads, its cool and its bees.
432.nuance: Continues the list of 431; the repeated verb endings give a litany of trees rather than a sentence.

433.reading: More trees of the grove are named by the look of their shoots and flowers: iluppai, madhuka, kaithai and punnai among them.
433.nuance: Two or three tree names here are doubtful in the edition's word division.

434.reading: Creepers and climbing flowers are listed: jasmine, mullai, madhavi and kokudi with buds and clusters, and a flowering pond among them.

435.reading: The grove's open flowers are listed again: kongu, punnaga, ilavam and patiri, whose petals open beyond counting.

436.reading: In the grove's flowers bees, koels and mynas take their pleasure, and the verse ends by saying the grove's blossoming was such as to delight those who delight in fate and mind.
436.nuance: The last line, which seems to say the sight pleased minds that delight in fate, is read with doubt; விதி மகிழ்பவர் is not clear from the edition's division.

437.reading: A garlanded man, pleased at the sight, hears birds call him to come here, and enters the bank of a pond where flowers open.
437.nuance: The man is named only by his garland (அலர்தாரவன்) and by the verb; the story elsewhere gives him a name this verse does not.
437.event: The garlanded man enters the bank of the flowering pond.

438.reading: The pond's bank, wet with spray, is heavy with flowers and rising bees, and the south wind comes to meet the place.

439.reading: Where the water, the pearl-strewn sand, a gold-bright altar and bright fire-like flowers meet, the man sees an asoka tree.
439.event: The man sees an asoka tree beside a shining altar.

440.reading: As he reaches its shade, the keeper of it tells the flowers to scatter and bloom, and shows a gem-bright slab, saying many things in wonder at what it is.
440.nuance: Who is meant by the one who says 'what is this' (line 4) is not settled by the verse.
440.event: The keeper welcomes the man and shows him the gem slab under the asoka.

441.reading: The keeper tells him, wearer of the garland, that this gem-stone, made to be a shaded seat for him, is pleasing to climb, and bids him sit gladly.
441.nuance: The speaker is taken from the keeper of 440 and the addressee from the vocative 'wearer of the garland' (தாரோய்); the verse does not name either.
441.event: The keeper offers the garlanded man the gem slab as his seat.

442.reading: The one who came down from the shining sky says he cannot think how a tree of fire-bright flowers could cast a shade, and asks whose golden place it is in the grove-god's precinct and how he came to enter it.
442.nuance: Whether the descender is the garlanded man of 437 or another is held open by the edition's compression.
442.event: The man who has come down from the sky asks what the place is and how he came to enter.

443.reading: The keeper answers that the slab is not to be thought of as a god's; no one but the anklet-wearers addressed is fit for it.
443.nuance: The plural 'you with anklets' (கழற்றகையினீர்) shows more than one hearer; the verse does not say who they are.
443.event: The keeper says the slab belongs by right to those he addresses.

444.reading: The keeper begins to say how the slab came to be, and reports that a learned house-priest of the city's lord had once spoken of it.
444.nuance: The priest's name is garbled in the edition's division (பொன்னருவி and an unclear second name).
444.event: The keeper reports that the king's priest foretold the slab.

445.reading: The priest had said that a fierce, spear-carrying lord of the Vidyadhara world would come seeking a bride for the king's son and descend here this very day.
445.nuance: The report is relayed by the keeper and the speaker of 'என்றான்' is the priest only by the story so far.
445.event: The priest foretells a Vidyadhara lord's coming to seek a bride for the king's son.

446.reading: The priest added that the youth would destroy him, the foe of a lion-slaying man, when he came blazing in anger with his discus, so that the one he faced would tremble.
446.nuance: The enemy and the youth are not named; the identification with the story's hero and his foe is from the larger book, not this verse.
446.event: The priest foretells the youth will overcome the discus-bearing enemy.

447.reading: After he has killed his enemies, the youth will make this shaded slab, and when he descends is to be received, so the priest said; the keeper has stayed to wait.
447.nuance: The line 'நீங்கலன் இருந்தனன்' makes the keeper's waiting part of the fulfilment.
447.event: The keeper has waited at the slab as the priest foretold, to greet the one who descends.

448.reading: When the keeper has finished, the king sends four goddess-like women after the man who has eaten and sits there, to ease his journey's weariness.
448.nuance: Whether the guest has eaten what the keeper offered or merely rested is not clear from அருந்தனன் in line 1.
448.event: The king sends four women to attend the seated guest.

449.reading: The four women walk like swans, their gem girdles and anklets ringing, ear-ornaments glinting, and flowers slipping loose in their hair.
449.event: The four women walk toward the guest.

450.reading: As the women walk, their arm-garlands swing, their brow-bows rise in alarm and their sword-sharp eyes outdo the deer's in pride.
450.nuance: The brow-as-bow and eye-as-sword images are the poet's description of the women's bodies, not an event.

451.reading: The women's red-dyed feet and ringing anklets, their girdled hips, pearl-hung breasts and gait confuse the peacock in the hills.
451.nuance: The comparison is written as if nature were baffled by them; the grammar of lines 3 and 4 is read with doubt.

452.reading: Their peacock-tail girdles, spotted pairs of breasts and bending waists make a busy sight, and bees cry out and rise from them.
452.nuance: The verse is a compressed description of the women's bodies; its last line reads as the bees' lament.

453.reading: The power of their breasts and brows, of their lives' undoing and of every art of love is said to be marked in the killing look of their sword-like eyes.
453.nuance: The verse treats the eyes as the sign of the love-god's whole equipment, at which breasts and bow-brows are only instruments.

454.reading: Their lips tremble and their pearl-teeth smile, sweat beads their foreheads, earrings shine and their curled hair meets their brow-marks, as they shape their faces' work with a thin glance.
454.nuance: The verse ends the chapter on the women's approach, with the message they are sent to deliver not yet spoken.
454.event: The four women shape their faces' play toward the guest.

links.note: 447 has the priest foretell the slab; 441 has the keeper offer it as a seat made for the man.
links.teaches: The offer in 441 is the fulfilment of the foretelling in 447, so the keeper is shown acting from a prophecy and not on his own.

links.note: 176 draws spring as a copy of women; 451 has the women confuse the peacock with their gait.
links.teaches: One image runs both ways: spring is drawn from women's bodies in 176, and in 451 women outdo nature, so the poet changes which side is the model.

links.note: 450 sets the women's eyes above the deer's; Kural 1085 finds the deer, the eye and Death all in one look.
links.teaches: The epic uses the same deer-and-eye comparison as the couplet but lets the deer lose, where the couplet lets the look hold the deer's frightened shyness as one of its three natures.

gains.a: The women's eyes get the couplet's three-natured look, so the poem's deer is more than a measure of beauty: it is something the look can frighten.
gains.b: The deer-eye comparison shown at work in a procession where a king sends the women out for a purpose, rather than a lover's chance meeting.

links.note: 453 calls the women's sword-like eyes the mark of every killing art of love; Kural 1083 learns what Death is from a woman's large war-making eyes.
links.teaches: Both name the glance as a killer, but the couplet is one man's astonished cry and the epic makes it a settled doctrine of the women's whole equipment.

gains.a: A first-person confession that the eyes kill, which the epic's catalogue states only as a fact of their bodies.
gains.b: A general rule about what such eyes carry, given as the sum of breasts, brows and arts rather than the eyes alone.

links.note: 453 hails the women's eyes as the killing sign of love; Naladiyar 44 refuses the sword-and-lily praise and sees only a scooped-out palm fruit.
links.teaches: The two cannot both stand: one accepts the eye as a weapon, the other denies the image on the ground that the eye is only flesh, and which holds depends on whether the speaker is praising or renouncing.

gains.a: Its praise of the eyes is shown to rest on a metaphor a renunciant would call blindness.
gains.b: The target of its refusal is given a full, dazzling form in a poem written to enjoy it.

links.note: 454 shows the women shaping the face's work with glance and smile; Siddhar 10 prays to forget women who show hand, eyes and face.
links.teaches: The siddhar's prayer names the same tools the epic's women use, as the lure to be forgotten, where the epic presents them as skill.

gains.a: The women's play of face is seen as what the renunciant fears, not only what the poet admires.
gains.b: Its infatuating gestures get a full picture of them performed, which the prayer names but does not show.

source_issues: Verses 431-436: the edition's word division runs words together, and several tree names are doubtful.
Verse 444 line 3-4: the priest's name is garbled (பொன்னருவி and an unclear second name).
Verses 440-447: the speakers are not named in the verses; the keeper, the descender and the priest are inferred from the sequence.
